author: angela-bouma
description: For centuries, tales of witchcraft got along fine without a broom. The object only arrives in the 15th century, when judges start believing in night flights to the sabbath.

hero.hook: A household tool became a monster's signature.

blocks.text: The witch on her broomstick is one of the most familiar images in Western folklore. Yet the link is far newer than witchcraft itself. For centuries, European stories spoke of magic and night spirits with no broomstick in sight. The classic image only appears at the end of the Middle Ages, above all in the **15th century**, when the authorities began hunting groups of witches, pacts with the devil and night flights.

Medieval theologians debated the question: do people really travel at night with a demon's help, or is it all illusion? In the early **13th century**, the theologian [[Roland of Cremona]] recorded tales of night journeys and magical ointments. It was an early link between witchcraft, altered consciousness and imagined flight, long before any broomstick.

In the early **15th century**, witchcraft accusations increasingly included a new idea: witches flew to nighttime gatherings, the [[sabbath]]. Flight solved a problem. It explained how witches scattered across dozens of villages could ever meet. Local suspicion became fear of a vast conspiracy.

Some early modern writers describe [[flying ointments]], made from plants like nightshade and henbane, which witches supposedly rubbed on before their night journeys. Those plants really can cause hallucinations and a sensation of flying, but no record proves that anyone ever flew.

The earliest known image of this belief appears in a manuscript of [[Le Champion des Dames]] (The Champion of Ladies), a poem by Martin Le Franc, from around **1440**. Two women fly across the page, one on a broom, the other on a plain staff. For the first time, flight, witchcraft and an ordinary household object were brought together.

blocks.caption: Two "Vaudoises" in flight, on a broom and on a staff. Margin of a manuscript of Le Champion des Dames, around 1440.

blocks.text: One of the first famous cases is that of [[Guillaume Edelin]], an Augustinian prior and doctor of theology near **Paris**, who had once spoken out against warnings about witchcraft. Arrested in **1453**, he confessed during his trial to practicing witchcraft and to riding a broom to the sabbath.

The confession, obtained under pressure, proves nothing about any supernatural flight. But it shows that the link between witch and broom was already circulating by the mid-15th century. The irony of the case: a skeptic ended up tied, through a forced confession, to one of witchcraft's most famous images. Edelin repented and spent the rest of his life in **prison**.

The broom carries meaning because sweeping is **women's work**. In medieval and early modern Europe, keeping the home clean was, by definition, a woman's job. Turning a cleaning tool into a means of flight follows a wider pattern: women's everyday tasks, cooking, healing, childbirth, were treated as the likeliest hiding places for dangerous magic.

blocks.caption: The Witches, by Hans Baldung Grien (1510): one of them rides a goat backwards, a fork in her hand.

blocks.text: The broom was never the only object people imagined witches riding: stories also mention staffs, animals and bundles of straw. If it won out, it is not because it is magically special. It combines **three qualities**. It is recognized at a glance, it evokes the home, it can be drawn in a single stroke. A flying tree can suggest supernatural travel. A woman on a broom reads instantly as witch.

The [[Enlightenment]] weakened the belief by changing how the supernatural was judged. Observation and evidence made demons and magical flight less plausible. Growing distrust of confessions obtained under **torture** undermined the legal basis for the trials. Educated Europeans saw it as superstition, and the trials became rare.

But the image did not fade with the belief. It moved into **art**, then theater, then film, until it needed no explanation at all. That is the real power of the symbol: an ordinary object, once loaded with enough fear and meaning, outlasts the belief that created it. Nobody believes in the witches' flight anymore, and the image has not moved an inch.

blocks.caption: Linda maestra, an etching by Goya (1799): an old witch and a young woman on the same broom.

blocks.text: The broom never made anyone fly: it served to explain the sabbath, to point at women, and then to recognize a witch at a glance, long after the trials were over.
